title: A mixing desk of learned faders
allegory: A linear layer is a mixing desk: each output speaker plays its own blend of every input channel, set by a row of faders plus one offset knob, and training is an engineer nudging those faders until the mix sounds right.
map: the fader for channel j on speaker i
one speaker's blend of every channel
output y_i: row i of W dotted with x
a fader never wired to the desk, so the engineer can't reach it
a tensor not registered as nn.Parameter, so the optimizer never steps it

cap.1: An MLP, an attention head, a probe: open any of them up and the same brick is inside. This film is about that brick.
cap.2: MLP layers, attention projections, linear probes and LoRA adapters are all built from one pattern: a learned matrix multiply plus a bias. Understand it once and most model code reads easily.
cap.3: nn.Linear computes y = xWᵀ + b with W of shape (out_features, in_features). Attention's Q, K, V and O maps, MLP layers, probes and LoRA factors are all learned linear maps of this kind.

cap.1: Picture a mixing desk. Each speaker plays its own blend of every instrument, set by its own row of faders, plus one offset knob. Training nudges the faders.
cap.2: Each output is a weighted sum of all the inputs plus a bias: one row of weights per output, one weight per input. Gradient descent adjusts every weight and bias.
cap.3: Output i is row i of W dotted with x, plus b_i. W has out_features rows and in_features columns, so the layer learns out×in weights and out biases.

cap.1: Read it as: take the inputs, run them through the faders, add the offsets. Every output is a blend of every input.
cap.2: PyTorch stores W as (out_features, in_features) and computes x @ W.T + b, so a batch of rows goes in and a batch of rows comes out. The bias broadcasts over the batch.
cap.3: For x of shape (batch, in), xWᵀ + b has shape (batch, out). Parameter count is out·in + out; print_param_count and torchinfo.summary check it against a reference before you train.

cap.1: Each row is one speaker's faders. A positive fader boosts a channel, a negative one subtracts it, a zero ignores it.
cap.2: Row i of W is output i's recipe. With x = (1, 2, 3), speaker 1 plays 0.5·1 − 1·2 + 2·3 = 4.5, plus its bias; speaker 2 plays 1·1 + 0·2 − 0.5·3 = −0.5, plus its bias.
cap.3: Each output is a dot product of a row of W with x, plus b_i, so each row is a direction the output measures x along. That is why a linear probe reads a concept as a direction.

chapters.name: The unwired fader
chapters.verdict: Count the parameters before you train.

cap.1: A fader that was never wired into the desk can't be reached by the engineer. It stays where it started, and the rest of the mix quietly works around it.
cap.2: PyTorch only trains what you register. Wrap weights in nn.Parameter and sub-layers in nn.ModuleList; a plain tensor or Python list is invisible to model.parameters().
cap.3: nn.Module routes Parameters into _parameters via __setattr__, and the optimizer gets whatever parameters() walks. Unregistered leaves can still collect .grad but are never stepped, moved or saved.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: An MLP: two desks with a bend between
A probe: one desk reading a direction
LoRA: a thin pair of desks beside a frozen one

cap.1: Once you see the desk you see it everywhere. Two desks with a bend between make an MLP, and a single desk can read a concept out of a model.
cap.2: MLP layers, attention projections, probes and LoRA adapters are all learned linear maps. Reading a model's weights mostly means reading matrices exactly like this one.
cap.3: Understanding and steering a model runs through these matrices: a probe's weight row is the direction a concept lies along, and each later layer reads the stream through its own W.

coda.title: Two desks in a row, with and without a bend between

caption.1: Move any slider. The blue line stays straight however you set the two desks. Only the orange one, with a bend between, can kink.
caption.2: Two linear layers in a row collapse to one: w2(w1·x + b1) is a line with slope w1·w2. The ReLU between them is what lets an MLP bend. Watch where the orange kink moves.
caption.3: Affine maps compose to an affine map, so depth without a nonlinearity adds nothing. The kink sits at x = −b1/w1: the bias decides where the unit switches on.

The unembedding: a linear map from the residual stream to one logit per token

hamming.what: A learned matrix multiply plus a bias: every output is a weighted blend of every input, plus an offset.
hamming.when: Whenever a model needs to mix features into new ones, which is almost every learnable step in an MLP or a transformer.
hamming.why: It is the simplest map that lets every output depend on every input with a learnable strength, and because it is linear it is the part of a model you can read most directly.

object.title: The fader desk
object.subtitle: Three speakers, four channels and an offset knob each: every bar is one term in a mix.

cap.1: Three speakers, four channels, plus an offset knob each. Every bar is one term in a speaker's mix: a fader times a channel.
cap.2: Each bar is one term W[i, j]·x_j; the last column is the bias b_i. A row's bars add up to one output.
cap.3: Bars show the per-term contributions of y_i = Σ_j W_ij x_j + b_i, laid out as an out × (in + 1) array.

cap.1: Turn up channel x2 and its bar grows in every speaker's row at once. Every output hears every input.
cap.2: Scaling x2 scales column 2 of the contributions: one input feeds all outputs through its own column of W.
cap.3: ∂y_i/∂x_j = W_ij for every i: a column of W is how input j fans out to every output.

cap.1: Silence x2 and it drops out of every mix. A zero fader or a silent channel both remove a term.
cap.2: A zero input or a zero weight removes that term from every sum it appeared in.
cap.3: Contribution W_ij x_j vanishes if either factor does; a zero column of W means input j is ignored entirely.

cap.1: Turn up the offsets. Each speaker shifts by its own constant, whatever the channels are doing. That is the bias.
cap.2: The bias adds a per-output constant that does not depend on the input, so the layer is not forced through zero.
cap.3: b makes the map affine rather than linear: y(0) = b. In a ReLU layer it sets where each unit switches on.

cap.1: Add up one row and you have one output number. The whole desk, every row at once, is one matrix multiply.
cap.2: Summing each row gives y. Doing all rows together is xWᵀ + b, one call on a GPU.
cap.3: Row sums give y = Wx + b; batched, it is a single GEMM plus a broadcast bias.

predict.q: A layer maps 784 inputs to 100 outputs. How many numbers does it learn?
predict.why: One fader per (output, input) pair plus one offset per output: 78,400 + 100 = 78,500.

predict.q: You stack two linear layers with nothing between them. What do you get?

options.t: A curvier function than either alone

predict.why: A blend of blends is still a blend: W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = (W2W1)x + (W2b1 + b2). You need a bend like ReLU between.

predict.q: You store a weight as a plain tensor instead of an nn.Parameter. What happens in training?

options.t: It never moves, and nothing complains
PyTorch raises an error straight away

predict.why: The optimizer only sees model.parameters(). An unregistered tensor is skipped silently while the loss still falls.
